senses: The process of becoming less active or severe.
ety: Latin subsidens, subsidentis, present participle of subsidere. Equivalent to subside + -ence.
examples: The subdual or subsidence of the more violent passions.

senses: Going or directed inward, entering.
Open to entry or examination.
ety: From ingress + -ive.
examples: The chances that your Internet activity is being monitored are low, despite the ingressive nature of the modern Internet environment.

senses: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.
To misrepresent.
To counterfeit; to forge.
To prove to be false.
ety: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.
examples: The Irish bards use to forge and falsify everything as they list, to please or displease any man.
By how much better than my word I am, / By so much shall I falsify men's hope.

senses: To take (someone) into one's confidence; to speak in secret with.
To entrust (something) to the responsibility of someone.
To say (something) in confidence.
ety: From Middle Scots confide, confyde (“to put trust in”), from Latin confīdere (“to put trust in, have confidence in”), from con- (“together”) + fidēre (“to trust”). First attested in English use in the early 17th century. Doublet of faith and fidelity.
examples: I could no longer keep this secret alone; I had to confide in my brother.
She confided in me about her plan to rob the bank.
I confide this mission to you alone.

senses: One who supports policy favouring war.
ety: From the minced oath by jingo, which was used in a music hall song, written ca. 1878 by G. W. Hunt, that supported Britain's then belligerent attitude towards Russia. In this context, a euphemism for Jesus, influenced by the meaningless presto-jingo used by conjurors. A connection with the Basque jainko (“god”) has been suggested, but evidence is lacking.
examples: He is the jingo of the universe; he will say, "My cosmos, right or wrong."
Spare me all the outrage and "pseudo jingo stuff" about Iran's imprisonment of our troops, said Peter Hitchens in The Mail on Sunday.

senses: That which sinks or descends.
One who sinks something.
A weight used in fishing to cause the line or net to sink.
A sinker nail, used for framing in current construction.
In knitting machines, one of the thin plates, blades, or other devices, that depress the loops upon or between the needles.
ety: From sink + -er.
examples: McLachlan's value as a coal miner was enhanced by the specialized skill he learned as a shaft-sinker.
Hook the sinker onto this loop.
Then the caplin moved off, and five minutes later there was no sound except the splash of the sinkers overside, the flapping of the cod, and the whack of the muckles as the men stunned them.

senses: Used for applying a mulch.
Used as a mulch.
ety: From mulch + -ing.
examples: This mulching mower can easily be converted to a bagging mower.
Compost is generally the best mulching material for the home garden.

senses: Having the consistency of goo: soft or viscous, and sticky.
Emotional or sentimental, especially to an excessive extent; mushy, soppy.
ety: The adjective is derived from goo + -ey (a variant of -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’)). The noun is derived from the adjective.
examples: The cookies, soft and gooey, proved a smash hit at the party.

You and your guests will get past the slight appearance problem when you taste the warm finished cake: the brown crust is like the ideal macaroon, and the center has the gooey, custardlike texture of a proper pecan pie.
It took months of baking and a lot of choc chips, but finally I cracked the perfect choc chip cookie—gooey in the centre, with a crisp edge and a caramelised nuttiness from the brown butter.

senses: An Italian restaurant.
ety: Borrowed from Italian.
examples: Americans who patronized these ristorantes for their liquor often developed a fondness for spaghetti and meatballs...

senses: One who griefs: a player who plays a game primarily to reduce other players’ enjoyment of it.
ety: From grief + -er. First attested in the early 2000s.
examples: First, be a tree; in other words, ignore the griefer. This approach can be very effective because most griefers want you to get pissed off, and if you don't, they may move on to more fertile targets.

senses: Of a motor vehicle: to rumble loudly, to roar.
To grumble, complain.
ety: Perhaps by confusion with chunter.
examples: The truck chundered and rattled.
As their rented van chunders along the highway, John′s voiceover is heard, contemplating the compulsion that drives men to continue using juvenile punk monikers into their mid-thirties.
He taxied his plane carefully to the end of the strip and then went further on, into the rough grass. Then, with full flap and maximum throttle, he came chundering along towards us.

senses: One who has a sexual fetish.
ety: From fetish + -ist.
examples: A social media convention among young and famous people is not to show bare feet to avoid attention from foot fetishists.

senses: Manly, masculine.
ety: From beard + -y. Compare Saterland Frisian boartich (“bearded”), Dutch baardig (“bearded”), German bärtig (“bearded”).
examples: The Doge is one of the popular barytone's most weighty performances, and we do not remember to have heard his voice more powerful, his acting more beardy and emphatic.

senses: Causing, or likely to cause, an uproar.
Characterized by uproar, that is, loud, confused noise, or by noisy and uncontrollable laughter.
Extremely funny; hilarious.
In a mess; dishevelled, untidy.
ety: From uproar + -ious (a variant of -ous (“suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree, commonly in abundance”)).
examples: The two bushes looked up in surprise, and when they saw Dorothy, the Cowardly Lion and Sir Hokus, they fell into each other's branches and burst into the most uproarious laughter.

senses: The state of being a whore, prostitution; sexual indulgence, fornication.
ety: From Middle English horedom, hordom, from Old Norse hórdómr, ultimately corresponding to whore + -dom. Cognate with Swedish hordom (“whoredom”), Middle Dutch hoerdom (“whoredom”).
examples: Force not your slave-girls to whoredom that ye may seek enjoyment of the life of the world, if they would preserve their chastity.

senses: A small empty or air-filled space or vacuity.
ety: From French vacuole, from Medieval Latin vacuola, formed as a diminutive of Latin vacuus (“empty”).
examples: This surface itself was not entirely homogeneous, but beneath it, seen as through ground glass, there were dim whitish patches or vacuoles, which varied constantly in shape and size.

senses: Beaked: having a beak.
Beak-like: resembling a beak.
Having a nose which resembles a beak.
Made using a beak; (of a sound) produced through a beak. (of a gesture)
ety: From beak + -y.
examples: Jim Carrey tells John Hiscock about his beaky new co-stars in 'Mr Popper's Penguins' and how he made it big.
The two men, who for more than sixty years had never been very much out of touch, were quite similar in appearance: spare of form, with beaky, weathered faces and strands of whitening hair.

senses: A particular region defined by its weather or climate.
The context in general of a particular political, moral, etc., situation.
ety: Borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “(zone of) latitude”, literally “inclination”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to slope, incline”). See also climate.
examples: After working hard all of his life, Max retired to warmer climes in Florida.
Is this the Region, this the Soil, the Clime, Said then the lost Arch-Angel, this the seat That we must change for Heav'n, this mournful gloom For that celestial light?
She thought of her husband in some vague warm clime on the other side of the globe, while she was here in the cold.

senses: A dance performed to ska, dub, or reggae music.
A style of rhythmic guitar strumming in ska, reggae, and punk.
ety: Originally Jamaican, attested from the twentieth century, but earliest source is uncertain. The verb sense be dishonest is evidently older. Perhaps originally onomatopoeic. The dance senses may come from a resemblance to motorcyclists weaving between larger vehicles. Compare skanker.
examples: All reggae dance represents a dialogue with that basic movement which is the skank — a kind of offbeat walking on the spot
He took it another step and brought blues into reggae music. I don’t play skank. I don’t play reggae guitar. So I had to call.

senses: A slum or shantytown, especially in Brazil.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Brazilian Portuguese favela.
examples: The favela is now the model for most of the world's cities, as vast numbers of people continue to migrate to them in order to survive.

senses: Excessively dramatic or emotional, especially with the intention to draw attention.
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting; scurrilous, shameful; wretched”), from Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting and the theatre”), from histriō (“actor, player”) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). By surface analysis, histrion + -ic.
examples: In the dance, the obsessive-compulsive keeps his mate endlessly frustrated. She, in turn, becomes more histrionic, and as she projects her emotional dirty part into him, he becomes more anal and compulsive.
A vicious circle may form in which the more rejected they feel the more histrionic they become, and the more histrionic they become the more rejected they feel.

senses: The lower edge of the side of the face (below the cheek), defined by the jawbone.
ety: From jaw + line.
examples: Sandra swooned over Pierce's manly jawline.

senses: A simple saddle girth used in Mexico.
Something that is very easy to do.
Something that is obvious or certain to occur; a sure thing.
A firm hold.
ety: Borrowed from Occitan cencha, from Latin cincta, or from Spanish cincha (“a belt or girth”), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum. Doublet of cingle.
examples: He found Andy morosely replacing some broken strands in his cinch, and he went straight at the mooted question.
We thought we had a cinch on getting out by way of this cord and so we followed that.
The job was a snap. I travelled the country averaging a thousand miles a week and, since the previous incumbent had been a lazy bugger, managed to treble the business. It was a cinch.

senses: A bet in which the bettor must select the first three placegetters of a race in the order in which they finish.
The attainment of three important achievements, qualities, etc.
A set of three related things, often things that cause problems.
The complete legislative and executive control of state or federal government by one party: governorship, the upper house, and the lower house of state or federal legislatures.
ety: From tri- + (per)fecta.
examples: The conservative player will play the exacta box bet and the occasional trifecta box wager.
In a trifecta, you must wager on three horses: the one that finishes first (win), the one that finishes second (place), and the one that finishes third (show) in order.
The money picture for Santorum could change after his trifecta win in Colorado, Minnesota, and Missouri Tuesday night.

senses: Someone who owns or runs a hotel.
ety: Borrowed from French hôtelier.
examples: Mumbai: Hotelier Gaurav Arya arrived at the Enforcement Directorate's (ED) office in Mumbai on Tuesday to record his statement in a money laundering case linked to actor Sushant Singh Rajput's death.
Jim managed to secure employment in a hotel on the lake shore, but even then I could see that his interest in being a hotelier was waning.
He was, by nature and choice, a hotelier and destined to become the most famous hotelier in the world.

senses: A white person.
ety: Borrowed from Swahili mzungu, from Common Bantu *mʊ̀díʊ́ngʊ̀.
examples: I have given my daughter to an mzungu, and he says he will make her like the wives of the white men.

senses: A steel reinforcing bar in a reinforced concrete structure.
A grid-shaped system of such bars.
ety: Blend of reinforcing + bar.
examples: The floor and walls for Copthall tunnel have already been constructed using formwork into which rebar (reinforcing bar) was placed, and then concrete poured.
The hash mark of rebar or the curve of a hubcap will create curious shapes to be decoded; even, perhaps, entire subway trains and lengths of tracks will remain.

senses: Inclined to sniffle.
Resembling a sniffle.
ety: From sniffle + -y.
examples: I've been sniffly all weekend; I think I've caught a cold.

senses: A foreigner, especially a British or a white person.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani फ़िरंगी (firaṅgī) / فرنگی (firangī), from Classical Persian فرنگی (farangī), from Old French franc. Doublet of franc.
examples: Prem, who knew him slightly from Dehra Dun (where Dhillon had been his junior), remembers Dhillon cheerfully telling everyone that the firangi were glad to have Indians patrolling their wire. This Prem doubted.

Then Kashibayi cleared her throat and told him, "Maharaj, our Babasaheb Sarkar was a very patriotic king who fought against the firangi fellows. He was betrayed by his own people who were shamelessly treacherous."

senses: A type of barbecued steak, popular in Latin America.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish churrasco (“barbecue”).
examples: Most of the old favorites--beef brisket, gumbo, churrasco, and Pine's famous Cajun green beans--are still around.

senses: A young sheep of either gender from about 9 to 18 months of age (until it cuts 2 teeth).
The meat of a young sheep.
ety: From Middle English hogget, from Anglo-Norman hoget and an Anglo-Latin hogettus.
examples: They sent a lorryload of hoggets to the auction mart, and they will keep the rest for their own flock.
They make a delicious dinner special of hogget. It is made with rosemary and mint.

senses: The process of being embrittled; loss of flexibility or elasticity of a material; the development of brittleness.
ety: From embrittle + -ment.
examples: Even if no weakening effects were noticed after one or two overheatings, the cumulative heat effects would cause embrittlement and failure after subsequent overheatings.

senses: Lying flat, face-down.
Emotionally devastated.
ety: From Middle English prostrat(e) (“prostrate”, also used as the past participle of prostraten), borrowed from Latin prōstrātus, perfect passive participle of prōsternō (“to prostrate”). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
examples: Prostrate fall / Before him reverent, and there confess / Humbly our faults.
Finally almost the whole world was combined against the evil-doers, who are now prostrate before us.

senses: The act of bending or flexing; flexion.
A turn; a bend; a fold; a curve.
ety: From Latin flexura. By surface analysis, flex + -ure
examples: The gular flutter is characterized by a rapid flutter of the gular region caused by flexure and relaxation of the hyoid apparatus

senses: Someone who participates in a marathon or other long-distance races.
ety: From marathon + -er.
examples: She called on all the marathoners to go to Staten Island to help with the clean-up effort and to bring the clothes they would have shed at the start to shelters or other places where displaced people were in need.

senses: An interwoven combination of parts or elements in a structure or system.
ety: Borrowed from Latin plexus (“a twining, plaiting, braid”).
examples: I have the sensation of being immersed in the very plexus of life, focal from whatever place, position or attitude I take my stance.

senses: Consisting of harsh, percussive, nonverbal sounds.
ety: From patho- + -genic.
examples: Melogenic music represents the wide middle area between the extremes of logogenic and pathogenic music.

senses: Having down, covered with a soft fuzzy coating as of small feathers or hair.
Low-spirited; down in the mouth.
ety: From down + -y.
examples: The chick's downy coat of feathers formed almost immediately to keep it warm.

senses: An addition or supplement modifying any official document, such as a treaty.
Any appendix or addition.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French codicille, from Latin cōdicillus, diminutive of cōdex. See code.
examples: If Nick answered a question Wani listened to him and then gave a flat little codicil or correction.

senses: To pound or beat rapidly or violently.
To pulse (often painfully) in time with the circulation of blood.
To exhibit an attitude, trait, or affect powerfully and profoundly.
ety: From Middle English throbben; possibly of imitative origin. Cognate with Scots thrab (“to throb”). Compare also drub.
examples: Her heart began to throb faster as the moment approached.
The bass in the song made the entire room throb with energy.
Having been married and divorced, Suzanne throbs with attitudes of strength, liberation and equality.
